posts.name: The AI Investor
posts.text: Not a bad idea, who has the guts to stand up for their leader?

quoted.text:
NVIDIA employees: go on strike. Now.

Not for a raise. Not for more PTO. For your founder.

Jensen Huang was just pushed out in four days, after thirty-three years building the company. The GPU, CUDA, the entire infrastructure the world's AI runs on today. And it ends with a three-line press release on a Thursday morning.

Here are the facts. Sunday, Huang admits to an affair and apologizes to his teams. The board launches an independent investigation, led by Wachtell Lipton and a former federal prosecutor. Thursday, he resigns under pressure. The investigation hasn't reached any conclusion. No technology leak has been established. No misconduct has been announced.

The sentence came before the verdict.

Let me be clear: if the investigation shows that NVIDIA secrets ended up in Beijing, he has to go, and nobody will defend him. But you don't unplug the most important builder of the decade over press reports and a market panic. It's called the presumption of innocence. It applies to founders too.

And it has worked before.

November 2023. OpenAI's board fires Sam Altman on a Friday night. Within days, more than 700 of roughly 770 employees sign a letter: bring Altman back, or we all walk. Five days later, Altman is back, and most of the board that fired him is gone.

Call it the Altman precedent: in a company built on talent, real power doesn't sit with the board. It sits with the people who build.

NVIDIA's engineers hold that power today. They're the ones running the machin

Stephen A. Smith: “Before I let you get on out of here, shifting, Jensen Huang.”

Stephen A. Smith: “Should he have stepped down?”

• Nvidia’s Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, president and director, effective immediately. CFO Colette Kress becomes interim CEO; Harvey Jones becomes board chair. Networking growth is translating into a materially larger sales base.

• Nebius reported Q3 revenue of $980.8M, up 571%, but now expects 2026 revenue at the low end of its $3.0–3.4B range. Remaining New Jersey capacity for Microsoft slips to Q2 2027. Next year’s $12–13B revenue outlook requires $40–45B in capex: power delivery remains the gating factor.

• SpaceX announced $74B of planned data-center investment: $24B near Starbase, Texas, and $50B in Cochise County, Arizona. The Texas campus would generate its own power; Arizona still needs county approval. This is a massive prospective infrastructure pipeline, not an immediately energized addition to AI computing capacity.

• Applied Materials finished fiscal 2026 with $34.4B in revenue, up 21%, and adjusted EPS of $12.89, up 37%. Semiconductor Systems sales rose 22% to $26.1B; services grew 20% to $6.9B. Equipment and installed-base spending both expanded, giving the growth story more breadth than new tool shipments alone.

• Siemens raised its medium-term comparable revenue growth target to 7–11%, from 6–9%, after annual orders reached €108.2B and backlog hit €143B. Smart Infrastructure targets 11–13% comparable growth in fiscal 2027. Electrification and data-center demand are supporting higher ambitions beyond the chip and server suppliers.

• Vertiv introduced PowerNexus MV UPS, an outdoor medium-voltage system targeting grid interconnection and AI load smoothing, with shipments expected from mid-2027. Peak efficiency reaches 98.5%; integration with long-duration batteries can support up to four hours of backup. Moving power protection outdoors also frees indoor space for compute.

🚨 La Chine a entraîné ses meilleurs modèles d'IA sur des puces Nvidia 

C'est ce qu'affirme Will Depue, ex-chercheur d'OpenAI, et sa méthode est assez folle

Quand on crée un modèle d'IA, ses poids partent de valeurs « aléatoires ». Sauf que ce hasard n'en est pas vraiment un : il dépend du GPU exact utilisé. Chaque puce laisse une empreinte, un peu comme une empreinte digitale, et cette trace survit jusque dans le modèle final publié

Il a testé plus de 6 000 milliards de combinaisons sur les modèles open source chinois. 
Le résultat est assez insane : DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3 et MiniMax-M3 portent l'empreinte de Blackwell, la puce la plus avancée de Nvidia, interdite à l'export vers la Chine

Et il l'a vérifié en vrai. Sur un B300, il retrouve à l'identique, bit pour bit, les poids de départ de DeepSeek. Sur un H100, rien ne correspond

Selon son estimation :

> 2 000 à 3 000 GPU Blackwell par modèle
>150 à 200 M$ par cluster
> plus d'un demi-milliard de dollars de puces interdites, rien que pour ces labs

Ce que ça change en vrai : 

1️⃣ Les contrôles à l'export américains fuient, très probablement via des pays tiers ou du cloud loué à l'étranger, c'est la thèse du DoJ sur Alice Huang et Megaspeed
2️⃣ Le récit « DeepSeek fait aussi bien avec moins de compute » prend un sérieux coup (cc les prochina)
3️⃣ La pression monte sur Nvidia et ses revendeurs, en pleine transition après le départ de Jensen et à quelques jours des résultats du 17/11

Il dit que des chercheurs "seniors"  d'OpenAI et d'Anthropic ont vérifié ses résultats. Si ça se confirme, Washington va être furieux

quoted.text:
I have a major result to share.

I’ve found conclusive forensic evidence that the top 4 Chinese AI labs—DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group—have built their newest models on NVIDIA’s most advanced Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China.

This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it. When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern—a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model.

Again, this evidence isn’t based on any insider information or leaking. It’s based on a forensic analysis of the model weights released by the companies themselves.

I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models. In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models—including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3—were initialized on NVIDIA Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in NVIDIA’s flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems.

I then verified these results on real hardware. Running unmodified PyTorch with the seeds I’d recovered, a Blackwell B300 reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s untouched starting weights bit for bit, and a rented GB200 reproduced Kimi

Beside Eric's book, another great book to read on this subject is The Evil Princes of Martin Place: The Reserve Bank of Australia, the Global Financial Crisis by Chris Leithner https://link.amazon/B0fjSEtsf

Although seemingly written for Australians (Martin Place is the home of the Reserve Bank of Australia), the book primarily uses US sources.

Chris shows the positive effects of little to no inflation for the first two centuries of America's existence, namely peace and prosperity.

posts.name: Faisal Islam
posts.text:
Interesting: Q3 GDP number was a tiny fraction of a per cent away from being 0.8%… about £37m away from registering officially best quarterly growth outside pandemic since 2017… it’s basically 0.75%

Also some people were asking about per capita. It was 0.7% per capita. At 0.6, 0.5, 0.7 this year, that is the strongest three-quarter per capita GDP growth outside of pandemic rebound since 2017.

Others were rather curiously suggesting this growth is all government spending. This is not the case in any of the data today. 2026 data shows growth in private sector business investment especially driving GDP growth, Govt share constant, now lower,  as Bank of England declared and showed in a chart last week (the purple bit).

“Unlike over 2022–25, when GDP growth was supported to a larger extent by rising public sector output, resilience this year has been primarily driven by the private sector, and in particular private sector services”: BoE MPR, last week.

BoE study last week was seeking to measure AI influence, but actually it also constructed useful measure over time for Govt share too from this data source in the monthly GDP data: https://www.ons.gov.uk/file?uri=/economy/grossdomesticproductgdp/datasets/contributionstomonthlygdp/current/contributions20261112.xlsx

Latest quarterly figures are even less dependent on government contribution, and more on private sector, also true across 2026… basically a tenth or less of total growth (ie even smaller purple bit below when updated to September), same share as 2012-2019, and way lower than 2022-2025, more like a third to a half (see chart below).

Also corroborated by fact Government consumption grown 1.1% this year against 1.9% for GDP (first time I can see this is lower than whole economy growth since 2022). Market-sector GVA (so ex-government), is up faster on year than whole economy.

Curious to see any data basis for claiming this current better growth is government spending-led.

quoted.text:
I think it’s time to revisit the accredited investor laws in the US.

Companies are staying private longer, where only accredited investors (aka rich people!) can invest. Retail investors can only come in after IPO, when much of the upside has already been captured.

These rules were created with the best of intentions, to protect regular people from scams - a noble idea. Unfortunately, in practice they've often made it illegal to get richer, unless you're already rich. A regressive tax!

We have to judge policies based on their outcomes, not on their intentions.

These are two possible routes I see:

1) Replace the rule with something merit-based, like a financial literacy test. Pass it and you're accredited. Having a qualification based on competency rather than your bank balance or income seems far more fair.

2) Remove the rule entirely. Let consenting adults assess their own risk. Disclosure requirements stay and fraud enforcement stays to punish bad actors.
